--- title: "Logistic regression" description: "Whether a species is there is a yes-or-no question, best answered with a probability. Logistic regression keeps that probability between 0 and 1, and turning it into yes or no is a choice the data cannot make for you." order: 4 categories: [supervised, classification] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## A probability stays between 0 and 1 Whether a species is present at a station is a yes-or-no outcome, and the most useful answer is a probability: how likely the species is to be there. Linear regression cannot give one, because its line runs above 1 and below 0 as easily as it ran below zero animals on [Linear and polynomial regression](linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd). **Logistic regression** keeps the weighted sum and squeezes it between 0 and 1. Turning the probability into yes or no takes one more choice, which the data cannot make for you. The survey's yes-or-no outcome is the count cut at zero: present if any animal was caught. That keeps where the species occurs and loses how many: a station with one animal and a station with the largest catch are both simply present. Cut a quantity into categories only when the question itself is yes or no, such as a legal limit or a protocol that records only whether a species was seen. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Logistic regression predicts the log-odds A probability $p$ must lie between 0 and 1, but a weighted sum of inputs can take any value. Logistic regression connects the two through the **odds**: the probability that something happens divided by the probability that it does not, $p / (1 - p)$. A probability of 0.8 gives odds of 4, often said "four to one". The odds run from 0 upwards without limit, and their logarithm, the **log-odds**, from far below zero to far above, the same range as a weighted sum. So logistic regression predicts the log-odds: $$\log\!\left(\frac{\hat{p}}{1 - \hat{p}}\right) = a + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots \qquad\text{so}\qquad \hat{p} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(a + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots)}}$$ However large or small the sum, $\hat{p}$ stays between 0 and 1. Against one input it traces an S-shaped curve, close to 0 at one end and close to 1 at the other. A squared input gives the log-odds one peak, as it did for counts, and the probability peaks at the same place. As with the [multipliers](count-regression.qmd#each-coefficient-is-a-multiplier) of Poisson regression, raising $e$ to the power of a coefficient gives a multiplier, here on the odds: the **odds ratio**. What it does to the probability depends on where the probability starts. An odds ratio of 2 takes a probability of 0.5 to 0.67, but 0.9 only to 0.95. ## A probability is not yet an answer Many uses need yes or no: survey a site or not, protect an area or not. A **threshold** turns the probability into an answer: yes if the probability reaches it, no if not. `predict()` uses 0.5, but nothing in the data chooses that number. A yes-or-no answer can be wrong in two ways. A **false alarm** says yes where the truth is no; a **miss** says no where the truth is yes. Raising the threshold gives fewer false alarms and more misses, and lowering it the reverse. The right balance depends on what each mistake costs, which only the person using the model can say. ::: {.diagram} ![Logistic regression predicts the log-odds with a weighted sum, as a straight line. The S-shaped curve turns the log-odds into a probability between 0 and 1. A threshold turns the probability into yes or no.](img/logistic-model.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Log-odds, a straight line: log-odds equals a plus b times the input; a rising straight line crosses a dashed line marking zero; the weighted sum can take any value, as a straight line does. Probability, squeezed between 0 and 1: p equals 1 over 1 plus e to the minus log-odds; an S-shaped curve rises from near 0 to near 1, between dashed lines at 0 and 1, with observed no answers as dots along the bottom and yes answers along the top, more of them to the right; the curve nears 0 and 1 but never crosses them. Answer, a threshold you choose: yes if p is at least the threshold; a dashed line at 0.5 cuts the curve, inputs to the left of the crossing are called no and to the right called yes; raising the threshold gives fewer false alarms but more misses. A note says a probability stays between 0 and 1, and turning it into yes or no is a separate choice."} ::: ## Worked example The outcome is `present`. The data, the split by site and the recipe with squared depth and temperature are those of [Linear and polynomial regression](linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd). In R, `logistic_reg()` predicts the probability of the outcome's second level. The survey lists `yes` before `no`, so `fct_relevel()` puts `no` first and the model describes presence rather than absence. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() |> mutate(present = fct_relevel(present, "no")) split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) predictors <- present ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season curve_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_relevel(substrate, ref_level = "sand") |> step_poly(depth_m, temperature_c, degree = 2, options = list(raw = TRUE)) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, PolynomialFeatures from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train, test = survey.iloc[train_rows], survey.iloc[test_rows] def squared(column): return (column, Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)), ]), [column]) curve_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ squared("depth_m"), squared("temperature_c"), ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), ["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop=["sand", "spring"], sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) ``` ::: ::: ### Logistic regression keeps every probability below 1 `logistic_reg()` takes the same recipe as linear regression. In scikit-learn, `LogisticRegression` sorts the classes alphabetically, so the second column of its probabilities is `yes`; `C=np.inf` turns off a penalty that [Regularisation](../05-generalisation/regularisation.qmd) explains. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} logistic_fit <- workflow(curve_recipe, logistic_reg()) |> fit(train) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression logistic_fit = Pipeline([ ("recipe", curve_recipe), ("model", LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, solver="newton-cholesky")), ]).fit(train[predictors], train["present"]) ``` ::: ::: The probability of presence peaks at 8.9 °C and falls away on either side. Linear regression with the same inputs, fitted to presence coded as 1 and absence as 0, predicts a probability above 1 for 4 of the 202 test stations; logistic regression cannot. Its coefficients read as odds ratios: with the other inputs held fixed, the odds of presence on mud are 1.62 times those on sand. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} temp_range <- range(train$temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE) grid <- tibble( temperature_c = seq(temp_range[1], temp_range[2], length.out = 200), depth_m = median(train$depth_m, na.rm = TRUE), chlorophyll_mg_m3 = median(train$chlorophyll_mg_m3, na.rm = TRUE), salinity_psu = median(train$salinity_psu, na.rm = TRUE), substrate = factor("sand", levels = levels(train$substrate)), season = factor("summer", levels = levels(train$season)) ) ggplot(augment(logistic_fit, grid), aes(temperature_c, .pred_yes)) + geom_jitter(data = train, aes(temperature_c, as.numeric(present == "yes")), width = 0, height = 0.03, alpha = 0.3, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_line(colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], linewidth = 1.1) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Probability of presence", title = "The probability of presence rises and falls with temperature") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The predicted probability of presence across the survey's temperatures, with the other inputs held at their typical values (sand, summer, median depth, chlorophyll and salinity). The points are the training stations, where the species was present (top) or absent (bottom).](logistic-regression_files/figure-html/fig-curve-1.png){#fig-curve fig-alt='A curve of the predicted probability of presence against temperature. It rises from about 0.1 in the coldest water to a peak of about 0.85 in the middle of the range, then falls again in warm water. Training stations are drawn as points along the top, where the species was present, and along the bottom, where it was absent; the points along the top are far more numerous, and the ones along the bottom are spread across the whole range.' width=1500} ::: ::: ::: Outside the sampled temperatures the curve carries on towards 0 in both directions, whatever the species does there; [Uneven sampling and extrapolation](../06-assumptions-limitations/sampling-and-extrapolation.qmd) deals with predicting outside the data. ### The threshold trades false alarms for misses **Accuracy** is the share of answers that are right. Each row below applies one threshold to the test sites. A threshold of 0 calls every station present, the answer a model would give if it had learned nothing. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} predicted <- augment(logistic_fit, test) calls <- function(threshold) { called <- predicted$.pred_yes >= threshold present <- predicted$present == "yes" tibble(threshold, called_present = sum(called), false_alarms = sum(called & !present), misses = sum(!called & present), accuracy = round(mean(called == present), 2)) } thresholds <- map(c(0, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9), calls) |> list_rbind() thresholds ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| threshold| called_present| false_alarms| misses| accuracy| |---------:|--------------:|------------:|------:|--------:| | 0.0| 202| 51| 0| 0.75| | 0.5| 181| 34| 4| 0.81| | 0.7| 158| 23| 16| 0.81| | 0.9| 60| 6| 97| 0.49|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} probability = logistic_fit.predict_proba(test[predictors])[:, 1] present = (test["present"] == "yes").to_numpy() def calls(threshold): called = probability >= threshold return { "threshold": threshold, "called_present": int(called.sum()), "false_alarms": int((called & ~present).sum()), "misses": int((~called & present).sum()), "accuracy": round((called == present).mean(), 2), } pd.DataFrame([calls(threshold) for threshold in [0, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | threshold | called_present | false_alarms | misses | accuracy | |------------:|-----------------:|---------------:|---------:|-----------:| | 0 | 225 | 47 | 0 | 0.79 | | 0.5 | 210 | 34 | 2 | 0.84 | | 0.7 | 171 | 23 | 30 | 0.76 | | 0.9 | 43 | 4 | 139 | 0.36 | ::: ::: ::: Calling every station present is right 75% of the time, because the species is common. The default threshold of 0.5 raises that only to 81%, and it still gives 34 false alarms, against 4 misses. At 0.7, the false alarms fall to 23 and the misses rise to 16; at 0.9, to 6 and 97. The model is the same in every row. If the map is used to protect the species, a miss leaves a site unprotected, and a low threshold suits. If it sends a vessel to sample the species, a false alarm is a wasted trip, and a higher one suits. For a rare species the default can fail completely: its probabilities may never reach 0.5, so nothing is called present. [Class imbalance](../06-assumptions-limitations/class-imbalance.qmd) takes this up. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Logistic regression predicts the log-odds of a yes-or-no outcome, so its predicted probabilities stay between 0 and 1; its coefficients read as odds ratios. - Turning a count into present or absent keeps where a species occurs and loses how many there are. - A threshold turns a probability into yes or no. Raising it gives fewer false alarms and more misses; choose it from what each mistake costs. - Compare accuracy with the answer that ignores the inputs: here, calling every station present was already right 75% of the time. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Refit the model without `step_poly()`, so temperature enters as a straight line in the log-odds. What shape does the probability curve take on the figure? 2. Fit the same model to `rare_species`, the species caught at about 5% of stations. What is the highest probability it gives any test station, and how many stations does the default threshold of 0.5 call present?
